en: And holds the sobbing Choro
Of no more account than his boot-heel.
No distinct words leave his mouth;
When they wail aloud, he hears no speech.
If called alive, he seems dead;
If called dead, he seems alive;
The lord and the Choro
Cannot come to an understanding.
For the sake of the tens of thousands,
Because the lord was gone from sight,
The Argyn-Kyrgyz people of Talas
Found the Ala-Too passes turned to mere roads,
And this nation was humiliated by all.
They mowed meadow grass as tribute,
And paid heavy taxes and levies;
What they saw was utter darkness,
And what they endured was a day of torment.
When the khan departed from the Kyrgyz,
Food vanished from their cauldron,
And their dear people lost their head.
No one could bear another,
No one heeded another’s words;
They drove away the noble lord with lamentation,
And clamored like plundering ravens.
Grief spread among the people,
And many were beaten and humiliated.
Such was the people’s degradation,
All their warriors became slaves,
And the people’s suffering became a commodity;
This honored hero here
Became a slave to one man after another.
Now this is the state of the people.”
Speaking thus, Külchoro
Seethed as his heart dissolved,
And, meeting the bloodthirsty warrior this way,
Told how the hills held deer and the plains argali,
Explaining the nature of the land;
Then of the walled city and the people at the gates
He told all that had happened,
Standing thus before the gray-maned lion.
And so Külchoro
Found the elder brother who had raised him,
The forebear dearer than a father,
His hobble-cord braided with gold,
The one he esteemed above
Both father and mother,
The fruit of the deep-rooted plane tree,
His lord whose figure loomed like a mountain.
Saying, “God has restored the magnanimous lord,”
The Black Giant stood rejoicing.
Külchoro stood there distraught,
From time to time crying aloud
And pleading for protection
As he begged his elder brother.
His elder brother stood unmoved,
And Semetey held all
His many golden, honeyed words
Of no more account than his boot-heel.
Speaking softly, then firmly,
Your wretched lion Külchoro
Let loose and began his speech.
Among the spearmen, this Choro
Possessed great prowess;
He could face six divisions of foes,
And possessed great strength.
The dark ridge with its lofty crest
Was truly a mountain pass.
He was the renowned, fortunate one,
Who, when the whole world made war,
Went forth alone into battle.
When he spoke, his words were lucid and clear,
Eloquent in speech and keen of sight—
Külchoro himself was plain and forthright.
Broad-jawed and fluent-tongued,
He was a great orator who never faltered.
From hellish torment and affliction
He had escaped many times.
Such was Külchoro’s nature:
He sharpened his dark tongue
And declaimed before the people;
Though the contest lasted months and years,
He neither stumbled nor tired;
Though humiliated and forced to plead,
He never let his hands and feet be bound.
His words spread like sugar;
He was created unlike other men.
He had received the people’s warrant
And the saints’ blessing.
Yet his heart would not soften upon the riverbank,
Nor would their blood mingle, though it boiled.
He had not seen that radiant face.
However eloquently Külchoro spoke,
He received no word of well-being.
He gave not the slightest answer,
Nor acknowledged the mighty warrior,
But tormented him with force.
He acted only through gestures,
His ears deaf and his eyes blind.
The poor, bewildered people
Had fallen into Külchoro’s hands,
There at the cave where they stood.
Külchoro kept hold of him,
Refusing to release his lord,
Holding his precious one motionless.
He held fast to his tent-pole,
And held his hero as a gift.
The precious falcon had been found,
And the beloved Choro’s precious
Honor was thus restored.
His grief dispersed and lifted;
Brave Külchoro’s
Once-blinded eyes opened,
And he beamed, crying, “Elder brother!”
The honorable kinsman-warrior’s
Moonlike face shone brightly.
Even now, to cross away like a spirit,
Semetey stood drawing back.
The Black Giant and Külchoro
Seized the bloodthirsty warrior together.
Külchoro stood thinking this:
“Long ago my khan and elder brother
Ruled the people and cared for the nation,
And was a great lord;
But now, today, my lion of an elder brother,
Speaking no words and uttering no speech,
Has become mute.”
Külchoro stood grieving.
“What I said has come true,” he thought.
“He would become a support at my waist.
You took me when I was a fledgling,
Saying, ‘My legacy left by the dear departed,
My child left by my khan and elder brother.’
You fondled and indulged me,
Never gainsaying my word.
You made your mother divide
The milk of her breast and nurse me.
Kicking together like colt and yearling,
Competing as we suckled her breast,
You made my cause one with yours.
Just when we were about to take
The two reins and single lead in hand,
And rule the entire world,
When, upon the earth the Creator made,
We were to live as sovereigns,
You dug my grave deep
And brought my sorrow thus to the boil.
You had my free hands bound,
Had my dark liver crushed,
And my hide of leather flayed.
Alas, because of you, bloodthirsty warrior,
Why was I beaten down
And plunged into so many sorrows?
Whatever I grasped became embers,
My lungs became leaden shot;
What I had not seen became blindness,
And I burned until I became black earth.
My horns broke, though my head remained;
I was ruined like a hornless beast.
Deprived of mane and tail,
Tormented, burning, and grieving,
I was ruined like a clay vessel.
Deprived of both hands,
For a time I was utterly wretched;
Deprived of both eyes,
For a time I was blind.
My turn passed and I was diminished,
I became the equal of a cripple,
A shriveled blind man.
From the beginning, this gray-maned lion
Was called the young gray-maned lion.
He was a hero and a lion;
Those who opposed him became black earth.
The stranger’s affairs prospered,
And the man who fought him vanished.
Such was Külchoro’s nature.
Unable to endure his fury,
He confronted his bloodthirsty lord;
The poor soul could not contain himself,
His heart burned and became flame.
Coiling like a venomous snake,
The warrior Choro, the gray-maned lion, grew fierce;
His heart burned into embers—
How could he possibly stand still?
Burning and blazing, he turned sideways,
And the noble Choro began to speak:
“You were a heroic, gray-maned lord,
The mighty protector on whom I relied.
No foe could overcome your snowy heights,
No enemy could advance against you.
You were a towering black mountain pass,
And I was the one who took shelter in you.
Hero, you were orphaned of your father,
You grew to manhood as an orphan,
And barely rejoined your people.
When you reached twelve years of age,
You became a blazing ember,
A leaping red flame.
You shattered royal camps and took their spoils,
And attacked mighty nations.
Sated with blood, you grew fierce,
And were named the bloodthirsty gray-maned lion.
You enriched the people of the valleys;
When those you hated fell into your hands,
You laid Khan Jakyp low.
You sent Köbösh into the grave
And revealed your gray-maned valor.
You conquered the Sary-Kaikan pass,
And seized every land your heart desired.
Hero, though I implored you, you ignored my words
And brought me to this wretched state.
My words sweeter than sugar—
You sought to break my back.
You passed through me like consuming fire;
From time to time,
You sought to blind my eyes.
Alas, my lord, you have not prospered;
You brought disgrace and humiliated me.
My heart sinks and I am torn apart:
If I call you alive, you are not among the living;
If I call you dead, you are not in the grave—
Why did you appear before my eyes?
You burned me until I was seared,
Blackened me into a coal,
And destroyed my precious life.
You revealed your mighty valor;
Without smoke and without flame,
You set me smoldering and burned me.
You began this grievous affliction.
On the uplands, the horses are piebald,
Thoroughbreds mingled with stallions;
You abandoned your livestock.
Fashioned with a shaft of gold,
You abandoned your throne.
Your speech is sweet and your words are honey;
Bloodthirsty lord, hear me without causing grief.
Do not loosen my shovel-like teeth,
Do not burn my heart like this.
Do not boil and burn into embers
The man who looked to you for protection.
I mourned and searched for many years;
Now that what I lost has been found,
How can I keep from dissolving,
When I have encountered my tiger, my elder brother?
My precious elder brother, begin to speak;
Lay aside your lordly pride.
Now I shall die at your hands—
The true realm from which none returns,
By the power of almighty Khidr-Allah.
Through twelve rearguards and forty scouts,
I offered my breast to bullets.
You made me suffer boundless affliction
And endure dreadful humiliation.
Famed Keng-Shor and Kan-Jailak,
Ülgülüü-Maral and Kümüsh-Tak,
The banks of Besh-Tash and Kapka-Tash—
You abandoned these lands.
